recommendations: WASH after every bowel movement — water cleaning (health faucet, bidet) rather than dry wiping with toilet paper; pat dry gently rather than wiping (wiping inflamed perianal skin causes more irritation)
Use moistened wipes (unscented, alcohol-free) rather than dry toilet paper in interim if water not available; dry toilet paper friction worsens perianal skin
Avoid scented soaps, talcum powder, and perfumed products in the perianal area (cause contact dermatitis worsening pruritus)
Wear breathable cotton underwear (prevents perianal moisture and maceration that worsen pruritus ani)

conservative_management.green_zone: Reducing symptoms with fibre, hydration, sitz baths; bleeding less frequent; no prolapse or manual reduction needed; satisfied with conservative treatment → continue; review at 4-6 weeks
conservative_management.yellow_zone: Persistent bleeding despite 4-6 weeks of conservative management; Grade II not improving; recurring acute episodes → GP/colorectal surgery referral for office procedure (rubber band ligation); proctoscopy to confirm grade; flexible sigmoidoscopy if >40 years
conservative_management.red_zone: Acute thrombosed external haemorrhoid with severe pain → urgent colorectal surgery within 24-72 hours for thrombectomy; Grade IV strangulated prolapse → emergency surgical referral; massive rectal haemorrhage → call 102/112 emergency

post_procedure.post_banding: Review at 4-6 weeks; assess response; rebanding if haemorrhoids persist; colonoscopy if not already done (particularly >40 years)
post_procedure.post_haemorrhoidectomy: Review at 2 weeks for wound inspection; sitz baths and metronidazole until wound healed; full healing 4-6 weeks; return to work: 1-2 weeks (office) to 3-4 weeks (physical labour)

complications.description: Acute clot formation in external haemorrhoidal plexus — causing dramatic onset severe pain and perianal swelling
complications.management: Thrombectomy within 72 hours (most effective); conservative after 72 hours (spontaneous resolution over 2-4 weeks)

complications.complication: Strangulation and Gangrene of Prolapsed Haemorrhoids
complications.description: Grade IV haemorrhoids trapped by anal sphincter → ischaemia → necrosis; extremely painful; systemic sepsis if gangrene develops
complications.management: Emergency surgical consultation; emergency haemorrhoidectomy if gangrenous; conservative reduction if possible under anaesthesia

complications.description: Gradual iron-deficiency anaemia from recurrent haemorrhoidal bleeding; often insidious; particularly significant in women with concurrent menorrhagia
complications.management: Iron supplementation; treat haemorrhoids definitively; colonoscopy to exclude concurrent malignancy as cause of anaemia

complications.description: Delayed bleeding (days 5-10 post-banding) when banded tissue sloughs off; usually minor; rarely significant haemorrhage requiring intervention
complications.management: Most resolve spontaneously; significant haemorrhage → urgent endoscopy and clot evacuation or re-banding

complications.description: The most common post-operative morbidity after haemorrhoidectomy; can be severe; most patients describe the 1-2 weeks post-operative period as the most painful experience
complications.management: Multimodal analgesia; oral metronidazole 400 mg TDS × 7 days (reduces pain); sitz baths; topical lidocaine; stool softeners (prevent hard stools tearing wounds); regular paracetamol + NSAID

complications.description: Severe constipation leading to hard impacted stool that cannot be passed — worsens haemorrhoidal symptoms dramatically; may require manual evacuation or phosphate enema
complications.management: Phosphate enema (Belix, Phosphate enema); manual evacuation under anaesthesia if severe; aggressive laxative regimen thereafter; identify and address underlying cause of constipation

complications.description: Chronic perianal itching from haemorrhoidal mucus discharge and soiling; leads to itch-scratch cycle further damaging the perianal skin; severely impacts quality of life
complications.management: Treat underlying haemorrhoids; perianal hygiene; avoid scratching; topical zinc oxide or hydrocortisone 1% short-term; treat secondary threadworm infection (common in children); skin biopsy if persistent to exclude lichen sclerosus or Bowen's disease (very rare but important)

complications.description: Rare but life-threatening bacteraemia and septic thrombosis of the portal vein following injection sclerotherapy, rubber band ligation, or surgery — particularly in immunocompromised patients; organisms from the contaminated perianal area seed the portal vein via the haemorrhoidal venous drainage
complications.management: Prevention: avoid haemorrhoidal procedures in severely immunocompromised (HIV AIDS with CD4 <100, post-chemotherapy, active inflammatory bowel disease); prophylactic antibiotics before procedures in high-risk patients; urgent IV antibiotics (broad-spectrum covering Gram-negative and anaerobes) if suspected

key_points: Extremely common — affects 25-35% of pregnant women; peak in third trimester and immediately postpartum
Most resolve spontaneously within 1-3 months post-delivery; conservative management is the primary approach

Safe treatments in pregnancy: ispaghula husk (Isabgol); lactulose; paracetamol; topical zinc oxide; witch hazel; sitz baths; topical lidocaine (short-term); Pilex ointment (Himalaya — short-term for acute episodes)
AVOID in pregnancy: oral diosmin/hesperidin (Daflon) — limited safety data; NSAIDs (third trimester); topical steroids in excess
Postpartum haemorrhoids that persist beyond 3 months should be reassessed for office procedures
Prevention: high-fibre diet throughout pregnancy (constipation prevention is the best haemorrhoid prevention); adequate hydration; sitz baths post-delivery for immediate perianal relief
Haemorrhoidal varices in cirrhosis are TRUE Porto-systemic anastomoses — not simple haemorrhoids — and can bleed massively
BANDING AND INJECTION SCLEROTHERAPY ARE DANGEROUS in portal hypertensive haemorrhoidal varices — risk of uncontrollable haemorrhage; only by experienced gastroenterologist with EMERGENCY BACKUP

Primary treatment is reducing portal pressure: propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker); TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) for severe cases; liver transplantation for advanced cirrhosis
Always check LFTs and look for liver disease signs in any patient with haemorrhoidal varices before any procedure
HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, organ transplant: all haemorrhoidal procedures carry higher risks of infection, impaired healing, and sepsis
Haemorrhoidectomy in HIV is associated with: prolonged wound healing; increased infection; anal stenosis; sphincter damage
CD4 count <200/mcL: avoid haemorrhoidectomy and banding; conservative management only
CD4 >200/mcL on antiretroviral therapy with good immune reconstitution: procedures can be considered with antibiotic prophylaxis; by experienced colorectal surgeon
Prophylactic antibiotics before any anorectal procedure in immunocompromised patients (co-amoxiclav 625 mg orally 1 hour before procedure)
Increasing constipation from: reduced mobility; multiple constipating medications (opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium channel blockers); reduced fluid intake; reduced fibre intake
Higher prevalence of Grade III-IV haemorrhoids from longstanding constipation; greater degree of prolapse
Surgical risk higher in elderly; office procedures preferred; PPH (stapled haemorrhoidopexy) has better post-operative tolerance than conventional haemorrhoidectomy
Concurrent digital rectal examination to exclude rectal cancer in all elderly patients presenting with rectal bleeding

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza causing severe coughing increases intra-abdominal pressure significantly — repeated strong Valsalva from coughing worsens haemorrhoidal prolapse and bleeding; patients recovering from influenza with acute cough episodes frequently experience haemorrhoidal flares; vaccination reduces illness burden and the associated Valsalva stress on haemorrhoidal tissue; particularly relevant for Grade III-IV haemorrhoidal patients
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All haemorrhoidal patients with Grade III-IV disease; elderly with haemorrhoids and limited cardiac/pulmonary reserve

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients with chronic haemorrhoidal bleeding may require multiple proctoscopic procedures and potentially surgery — exposure to endoscopic instruments creates small risk of healthcare-associated hepatitis B transmission in inadequately vaccinated individuals; portal hypertension from chronic hepatitis B causes haemorrhoidal varices; hepatitis B vaccination prevents the liver disease that leads to portal hypertension and haemorrhoidal varices
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All unvaccinated adults; all patients requiring anorectal procedures; all healthcare workers performing anorectal procedures

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes condylomata acuminata (anal warts) — a perianal condition frequently confused with external haemorrhoids and requiring completely different treatment; HPV also causes anal squamous cell carcinoma — a risk in high-risk populations (HIV, MSM, immunocompromised); HPV vaccination prevents the HPV strains responsible for anal warts and anal cancer; relevant for young adults and immunocompromised patients with perianal conditions being evaluated
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All young adults up to age 26 years (ideally before sexual debut); adults 27-45 years at increased risk; MSM; HIV-positive patients regardless of age

vaccinations_recommended.reason: COVID-19 frequently causes severe constipation and bowel habit changes (due to direct gut inflammation, immobility from illness, and opioid analgesic use) — both acute COVID and long COVID-related GI symptoms worsen haemorrhoidal disease; the dehydration and reduced mobility of severe COVID illness exacerbate constipation; vaccination reduces severe COVID and the associated gut dysfunction

when_to_see_doctor: ANY rectal bleeding — even if it appears typical for haemorrhoids; always requires clinical examination to confirm diagnosis and exclude cancer, particularly in patients over 40 years
First episode of rectal bleeding at any age — must be examined; haemorrhoids are a clinical diagnosis requiring examination, not an assumption
Rectal bleeding with ANY change in bowel habit (increased frequency, looser stools, alternating diarrhoea and constipation) — ALARM FEATURE; requires colonoscopy urgently
Rectal bleeding with unexplained weight loss — ALARM FEATURE for colorectal cancer
Persistent prolapse requiring manual reduction (Grade III) not responding to 4-6 weeks of conservative management — office procedure needed
Permanent prolapse unable to be reduced (Grade IV) — urgent colorectal surgery referral
Acute sudden onset severe perianal pain with a lump — possible thrombosed external haemorrhoid; urgent assessment within 72 hours for possible thrombectomy
Inability to walk or sit comfortably from anal pain — possible strangulation; urgent surgical referral
Fever with anal pain or swelling — possible perianal abscess or infected haemorrhoids — URGENT; perineal sepsis can be life-threatening

Anaemia (pallor, breathlessness) with rectal bleeding — haemorrhoidal bleeding causing significant anaemia; requires treatment of haemorrhoids AND investigation to exclude concurrent colorectal cancer
Soiling or faecal incontinence associated with prolapse — Grade III-IV haemorrhoids significantly affecting continence; specialist review
Pruritus ani not responding to 2-4 weeks of simple hygiene measures — exclude threadworms, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus; specialist assessment
emergency_signs: MASSIVE BRIGHT RED RECTAL HAEMORRHAGE causing weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness, or collapse — HAEMORRHAGIC SHOCK — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112) IMMEDIATELY; lie flat; IV fluid resuscitation; blood transfusion; emergency colonoscopy or surgical intervention

EXTREMELY PAINFUL PROLAPSED MASS AT THE ANUS with PURPLE-BLACK COLOUR and FEVER — STRANGULATED GANGRENOUS HAEMORRHOIDS — EMERGENCY SURGICAL REFERRAL; call 102/112; emergency haemorrhoidectomy may be required

ACUTE ONSET SEVERE PERIANAL PAIN WITH FEVER AND SYSTEMIC ILLNESS (rigors, extreme fatigue, confusion) — FOURNIER'S GANGRENE (life-threatening necrotising fasciitis of the perineum) or PERIANAL SEPSIS — CALL 102/112; emergency surgery mandatory; mortality very high without immediate debridement

POST-PROCEDURE SUDDEN BRIGHT RED RECTAL BLEEDING (after rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, or haemorrhoidectomy) causing dizziness or cardiovascular compromise — delayed post-procedural haemorrhage — EMERGENCY; call operating surgeon immediately; call 102/112 if cardiovascular instability
SIGNS OF HAEMORRHAGIC SHOCK with rectal bleeding — tachycardia >120 bpm, systolic BP <90 mmHg, pallor, cold peripheries — CALL 102/112

frequently_asked_questions.question: My doctor says I have piles but I am terrified it could be cancer. How can I be sure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Your concern is completely valid and understandable — rectal bleeding is genuinely a symptom shared by both haemorrhoids (very common and benign) and colorectal cancer (which must always be excluded). The answer depends on your age, symptoms, and examination findings. For patients under 40 years with classic haemorrhoidal symptoms (painless bright red blood on toilet paper, dripping after defaecation, not mixed with stool), confirmed haemorrhoids on proctoscopy examination (your doctor looking inside with a proctoscope), and no alarm features — haemorrhoids are the likely cause and colonoscopy is not always immediately mandatory. However, for ANYONE over 40 years with rectal bleeding; for anyone with changes in bowel habit alongside bleeding; for anyone with weight loss or anaemia; or for anyone with a family history of colorectal cancer — colonoscopy is MANDATORY to exclude colorectal cancer before assuming the bleeding is from haemorrhoids. In India, colorectal cancer is rising rapidly and presenting at younger ages than in the West. A colonoscopy provides complete reassurance by examining the entire large intestine. If you have been told you have haemorrhoids but are not fully satisfied with the investigation — it is entirely appropriate to ask for a colonoscopy or referral to a colorectal specialist. Never accept 'it's just piles' without a proper rectal examination and appropriate investigation for your age and risk profile.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I sit on the toilet for 20-30 minutes reading my phone every morning. Could this be causing my piles?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — absolutely. This is one of the most important and underrecognised causes of haemorrhoidal disease in modern India, particularly among young urban professionals. Here's what happens: when you sit on a Western toilet, the weight of your body and the pull of gravity on the pelvic floor cause the haemorrhoidal cushions to slowly descend downward. This descent is normal for a few minutes during defaecation, but when you remain seated for 20-30 minutes — even after you have finished defaecating — this prolonged downward pressure progressively stretches and weakens the fibromuscular supports that hold the haemorrhoidal cushions in their normal position. Over months and years, this destroys the ligaments holding the cushions in place, leading to permanent descent and prolapse. The 'mobile phone on the toilet' epidemic has genuinely worsened haemorrhoidal disease in India significantly over the last decade. The rule is simple: maximum 5 minutes on the toilet; defaecate efficiently, get up, and leave; the toilet is not a reading room. Additional help: put a small footstool (18-25 cm high) under your feet while sitting on the Western toilet — this mimics the more natural squatting position, reduces straining, and makes defaecation faster and more complete, reducing the time you need to spend seated.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Do spicy Indian foods cause piles? Should I stop eating spicy food?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Spicy food — particularly capsaicin from chillies — does not CAUSE haemorrhoids from scratch. However, if you already have haemorrhoids, spicy food can significantly WORSEN your symptoms. Here is what happens: capsaicin (the active compound in chillies) is not fully broken down in the digestive system and reaches the anal canal where it activates TRPV1 nerve receptors in the rectal and anal mucosa — increasing local blood flow, causing mucosal inflammation, and sensitising the area. This is why many patients with haemorrhoids notice that their bleeding, pain, and itching are significantly worse the morning after a very spicy meal. The practical advice: if your haemorrhoids are symptomatic — reduce chilli levels in your food, especially during flare-ups. You do not have to eliminate spicy food entirely or permanently — once haemorrhoids are treated, most people can return to their normal spice levels. Non-chilli spices (turmeric, cumin, coriander, black pepper — used at normal culinary doses) are actually anti-inflammatory and do NOT worsen haemorrhoids; many have beneficial properties for gut health. The real dietary priorities are INCREASING FIBRE (from whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and Isabgol) and DRINKING ADEQUATE WATER — these have far more impact on haemorrhoidal disease than reducing spicy food.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My doctor says I need rubber band ligation. Will it be painful and how long will it take to work?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Rubber band ligation is one of the most effective office-based treatments for Grade II-III internal haemorrhoids, and when performed correctly above the dentate line (the pain threshold in the anal canal), it should be essentially PAINLESS during the procedure. Here is what to expect: the procedure itself takes 10-15 minutes in the clinic; a proctoscope is passed, and a small rubber band is placed at the base of each haemorrhoidal cushion above the dentate line using a special device; you may feel a sensation of fullness or pressure but not sharp pain. However, over the next 24-48 hours, you may feel a dull aching discomfort from the anal canal — this is normal and managed with paracetamol and a warm sitz bath. Days 5-10: the banded tissue dies and falls off — you may notice some blood at this point (usually minor; occasionally more significant). IMPORTANT IMMEDIATE WARNING: if you feel SEVERE SHARP PAIN IMMEDIATELY during the banding procedure — tell your doctor immediately; this means the band has been placed too close to the pain-sensitive dentate line and must be removed and replaced. Regarding results: most patients notice reduced bleeding within 2-4 weeks; significant reduction in prolapse symptoms over 6-8 weeks. One session treats 1-3 haemorrhoidal cushions; you may need 2-3 sessions at monthly intervals for complete resolution. Success rate for appropriate Grade II-III haemorrhoids: approximately 75-85%.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I am 3 months pregnant with severe piles that are bleeding a lot. What can I safely do?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Haemorrhoids during pregnancy are extremely common — the growing uterus compresses the pelvic veins, progesterone relaxes vein walls, and constipation from iron supplements and hormonal changes all combine to cause haemorrhoidal flares. The reassuring news is that most pregnancy-related haemorrhoids significantly improve or fully resolve after delivery, and there are several safe treatment options: The most important thing during pregnancy is preventing and treating constipation — which is driving your haemorrhoidal symptoms: Isabgol (ispaghula husk) 1-2 teaspoons twice daily in plenty of water is completely safe in pregnancy and is the most effective stool softener; lactulose syrup is also safe; drink 2-3 litres of water daily; high-fibre foods (fruit, vegetables, whole grain roti). For symptom relief: warm sitz baths (15-20 minutes after each bowel movement in warm water) are safe and very effective for reducing pain and swelling; topical zinc oxide ointment or Pilex ointment can be applied for itching and discomfort; paracetamol 500 mg as needed is safe for pain throughout pregnancy. AVOID during pregnancy: oral Daflon (diosmin/hesperidin) — insufficient safety data in pregnancy; NSAIDs in third trimester; topical steroids for prolonged periods. Most importantly: almost all pregnancy-related haemorrhoids are expected to improve significantly after delivery. If haemorrhoids are still significantly troublesome more than 3 months after delivery, reassess with a colorectal surgeon for office procedures — it is very safe at that point.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between piles, fissure, and fistula? I am confused about which one I have.
frequently_asked_questions.answer: These are three different anorectal conditions that are often confused by patients (and sometimes even by non-specialist doctors) because they all affect the anal and rectal area. Here is a simple distinction: PILES (Haemorrhoids) — internal bleeding from enlarged vascular cushions above the dentate line; the main symptom is PAINLESS BRIGHT RED BLEEDING; you may also feel a lump come out during defaecation; generally NO SEVERE PAIN during defaecation (unless thrombosed). Think: 'bleeding without pain on defaecation.' ANAL FISSURE — a small tear or crack in the anal skin (below the dentate line); the main symptom is SEVERE SHARP BURNING PAIN DURING AND AFTER DEFAECATION (described as 'passing glass' or 'razor blade'); bright red bleeding (smaller amount than haemorrhoids); pain so severe many patients dread defaecation and withhold stool; most common in young adults; usually a midline posterior crack visible on gentle parting of the buttocks; typically treated with GTN 0.2% ointment, diltiazem cream, or botulinum toxin injection. Think: 'severe pain with defaecation and small amount of blood.' ANAL FISTULA — an abnormal tunnel (tract) connecting the inside of the anal canal to the skin around the anus; usually the result of an anorectal abscess; main symptom is DISCHARGE OF PUS (and sometimes faeces) from a small opening near the anus; chronic intermittent pain; may notice intermittent swelling that bursts and settles; NO SIGNIFICANT BLEEDING; treated surgically (fistulotomy or seton placement). Think: 'discharge and intermittent swelling near the anus.' These three conditions can coexist in the same patient (haemorrhoids + fissure is particularly common). Your doctor needs to examine you to determine which (or which combination) is causing your symptoms.
